narrative: A 24-year-old from Damascus who had studied English at university left Syria, first heading to Turkey to earn money for the journey onward to western Europe. In Istanbul, with little Turkish, he was mostly consigned to backbreaking labor until he had saved enough. By July he was ready and boarded a boat in Izmir, on the Aegean coast, bound for the Greek island of Kos, paying traffickers $1,200 for a crossing of only a few kilometers. In early August he took a ferry provided by the Greek government to Athens, then a bus toward the border with Macedonia. He crossed into Macedonia at Gevgelija, following the trail of thousands of others, and boarded a train across the country to the Serbian border. Up to that point the journey had gone more or less according to plan. Crossing into Serbia, traveling by night and through forests to avoid detection, the group was caught by Serbian border police and taken to a refugee camp in Presevo, where they were issued a 10-day visa. With the clock ticking and resources dwindling, he bought a bus ticket to Belgrade, stayed a few days, then headed north by train toward the border with Hungary. It took two attempts to enter Hungary. On the first, Serbian police caught him and others in a group of about 50 for overstaying their visas; the men and boys were taken to a police station and then to court, where the judge told them to either pay 50 euros per person to be released or wait about five days in prison. With time running out they paid the bribe. They then tried to cross at Horgos; heavy rain meant fewer police were on patrol that night, and they slipped across. Guided by the GPS on his phone, they walked through the forest for about five hours toward a specific gas station that had become part of an elaborate, makeshift migrant transport system, where Hungarian drivers waited to take migrants to a hotel in Budapest for 250 euros per person. The hotel was full of refugees and migrants waiting for vans to take them to Germany, or, for a lower price, to Austria. He paid about 600 euros per person, part of it for the driver and part for a Syrian middleman who took a cut for arranging it. The driver, an Afghan, promised to take them to a town just outside Munich, but instead dropped them at the border between Austria and Germany and told them to walk about 100 meters into German territory. On the advice of a friend he ended up at a refugee center in Sinsheim, in the southwest. In total he spent about $3,000 to reach Germany. He said the Germans had been good and he was sure of his prospects there, hoping to teach English.
